This paper studies an important and timely problem: how a user can determine whether a black-box LLM API is actually serving the distribution they believe it is serving. The paper formalizes this as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem, proposes MMD-based tests with string kernels, and empirically argues that a simple Hamming kernel is particularly effective in the low-sample regime. It then applies the method to commercial APIs serving Llama models and reports that a substantial fraction of endpoints appear distributionally different from Meta’s released weights. Overall, I found the paper interesting, practically relevant, and likely to stimulate follow-up work. The framing is clean, the empirical agenda is ambitious, and the API audit results are attention-grabbing. At the same time, there are several methodological and interpretational issues that should be addressed more carefully before I would be fully convinced by the strongest claims.

The main strength of the paper is the problem formulation. “Model equality testing” is a useful abstraction that unifies several practically important auditing questions: whether an API matches a claimed open-weight model, whether an endpoint drifts over time, and whether a provider has introduced modifications such as quantization or watermarking. This is a natural fit for statistical testing, and the paper does a good job motivating why benchmark accuracy under greedy decoding is insufficient when users care about sampled long-form outputs. I also appreciate that the paper explicitly targets the black-box setting without logprob access, which is the realistic regime for many commercial APIs.

A second major strength is the empirical comparison of candidate tests. The paper does not simply assert that MMD is appropriate; it compares several kernels and classical multinomial-style tests, and the results consistently suggest that the Hamming-kernel MMD is much more sample-efficient in the regimes of interest. The intuition is sensible: exact-match statistics are too sparse in high-dimensional completion spaces, while a positionwise similarity kernel can pool signal across many near-matching outputs. The experiments on quantization, watermarking, finetuning, and model swaps are broad enough to make the case that the method is not narrowly tuned to one distortion type. The release of code and a large completion dataset is also a meaningful contribution.

The API audit section is also compelling. Even if one discounts some of the stronger causal interpretations, the finding that many endpoints are statistically distinguishable from local reference weights under matched prompts and decoding settings is important. The paper’s emphasis on effect sizes via estimated MMD, not just binary rejection, is a good design choice. The qualitative examples, especially for Perplexity and some quantized variants, help make the phenomenon concrete.

That said, my biggest concern is that the paper sometimes slides from “distributionally different under our operational setup” to “the provider modified the model” or “the endpoint is not serving the claimed model,” and that inference is not always justified by the experimental controls. In practice, many factors besides quantization, watermarking, or finetuning can induce detectable distributional differences: hidden system prompts, chat template mismatches, tokenizer/rendering differences, undocumented stop sequences, server-side truncation, safety filters, speculative decoding artifacts, load-balancing across model snapshots, semantic caching, or imperfect implementation of temperature/random seeds. The paper acknowledges some of these issues, but the headline framing and some interpretations still risk overstating what the test establishes. The method detects non-equality of output distributions under a chosen prompt distribution and API interface; it does not identify the cause of the difference, and it does not necessarily imply substitution of a different base model. I think the paper should sharpen this distinction throughout, especially in the abstract, introduction, and audit conclusions.

Relatedly, the validity of the API audit depends heavily on how well the local reference distribution matches the provider’s intended interface. The appendix notes substantial effort to match chat templates and token counts, including using the Llama-3 template for Llama-3.1 because it empirically matched API token counts at collection time. This is reasonable, but it also highlights fragility: if the provider uses a slightly different prompt wrapper, hidden date injection, or system instruction, then the null is misspecified. In that case, rejection may reflect interface mismatch rather than model distortion. Since the paper’s central empirical claim is about commercial endpoints, I think this issue deserves much more prominence and perhaps additional robustness checks. For example, can the authors show sensitivity of rejection rates to plausible alternative local prompt templates? Can they compare raw-completion endpoints versus chat endpoints where available? Can they test whether flagged providers remain flagged under multiple reasonable prompt renderings?

A second substantial concern is the choice of Hamming kernel as the primary method. The paper is admirably transparent that this kernel induces only a pseudometric and can fail to distinguish distributions with identical positionwise marginals but different higher-order dependencies. However, the implications are more serious than the paper suggests. Since the Hamming embedding effectively captures per-position token marginals, the test may miss changes that preserve those marginals while altering syntax, discourse structure, or long-range dependence. This matters because some plausible API modifications, especially decoding-stack changes, could affect correlations more than marginals. The empirical success against the chosen alternatives is encouraging, but it does not establish broad adequacy. I would like to see either a stronger theoretical characterization of what classes of distortions the Hamming MMD is sensitive to, or at least a targeted synthetic experiment where Hamming provably fails and a richer kernel succeeds. As written, the paper’s recommendation of Hamming as the default may be too strong.

There is also a technical issue in Appendix A.1. The statement that MMD “satisfies triangle inequality, since MMD(P1,P3)=MMD(P1,P2)+MMD(P2,P3)” is incorrect as written. Equality certainly does not hold in general. Presumably the authors mean the square root of MMD corresponds to an RKHS norm and therefore satisfies the triangle inequality. But throughout the paper the notation appears to use the squared RKHS distance. This should be corrected carefully, because the distinction between MMD and squared MMD matters both mathematically and interpretationally. More generally, the paper should be more precise about whether reported quantities are squared MMD or its square root.

I also have concerns about the p-value calibration and testing protocol in the main experiments. In many places, the null distribution of the statistic is simulated by repeatedly sampling from a pre-collected dataset of completions from the reference model, rather than by fresh model calls. Since all experiments are effectively resampling from a finite empirical approximation to P, the test is not exactly operating under the idealized sampling model described in Section 2. This is understandable for cost reasons, but it introduces an extra layer of approximation that should be discussed more explicitly. In particular, if the reference dataset has finite support artifacts or collection-time biases, the simulated null may not reflect the true null. The permutation-based appendix helps, but it is limited in scale. I would like clearer discussion of whether type-I error is guaranteed only conditional on the empirical reference sample, or approximately under the true model.

The audit decision rule in Section 5 is also somewhat ad hoc. The paper tests against a composite null consisting of equality to either fp32 or fp16 local weights, then rejects only if both pairwise tests reject. This does control false positives in a simple way, but it is conservative and not obviously the most principled approach. More importantly, the final endpoint-level decision is based on repeating tests ten times and declaring failure if the average rejection rate is at least 0.5. This is not a standard hypothesis testing procedure, and its statistical meaning is unclear. Is this intended as a Monte Carlo estimate of power against a fixed endpoint? If so, the paper should say so explicitly and avoid presenting the thresholded result as a single formal test outcome. A more principled alternative might aggregate all samples into one larger test, or combine p-values across repetitions and prompt distributions using a standard method. As written, the “11 out of 31 endpoints” headline depends on a thresholding heuristic that deserves stronger justification.

Another limitation is the narrowness of the prompt distributions used for the main simulation study. The Wikipedia continuation task with random 100-character prefixes is a convenient long-form benchmark, but it is not obvious that it is representative of the kinds of prompts where API distortions matter most. The paper partly addresses this by auditing HumanEval and UltraChat for some models, which is good, but the core kernel comparison and sample-efficiency claims are still mostly based on Wikipedia continuation. Since the method is explicitly prompt-distribution dependent, I would like a more systematic analysis of how conclusions vary across domains, prompt lengths, and instruction styles. The appendix result showing power increases with the number of prompts is useful, but it does not substitute for diversity in prompt semantics.

The character-space evaluation for cross-tokenizer comparisons and API audits is practical, but it also changes the object being tested in a nontrivial way. Two models with identical token-level distributions but different detokenization conventions could appear different in character space, and conversely some token-level differences may be blurred. This is probably unavoidable for heterogeneous APIs, but the paper should be clearer that the tested equality is over rendered strings, not underlying token sequences. That distinction matters for the interpretation of “same model.”

I also think the paper could do more to separate statistical significance from practical significance. The MMD effect-size analysis is a step in the right direction, but the paper sometimes uses comparisons like “further from the reference than an entirely different language model” in a way that may overstate what the scalar MMD means. Since the Hamming MMD is kernel-dependent and prompt-distribution-dependent, such comparisons are operational rather than absolute. It would help to calibrate effect sizes more carefully, perhaps by relating them to concrete downstream changes across several tasks, not just HumanEval. The reported correlation with HumanEval accuracy is only moderate, which is itself an interesting result, but it suggests caution in interpreting MMD magnitude as capability degradation.

There are also some experimental details that would benefit from clarification. The paper says all samples are collected at temperature 1, but many APIs implement temperature and sampling differently, and some may silently clip or alter settings. Since this is one of the hypothesized causes of detectable differences, it would be useful to report whether the authors checked other temperatures or deterministic decoding. Similarly, the collection windows for some APIs span multiple days, which could confound “provider differs from reference” with “provider drifted during collection.” This is especially relevant because one of the paper’s motivating use cases is temporal drift. If possible, the authors should quantify within-provider temporal variability over the collection period, or at least discuss its potential impact on the audit outcomes.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has substantial merit. The core idea is strong, the empirical results are interesting, and the work opens a useful research direction at the intersection of LLM evaluation, black-box auditing, and nonparametric testing. My overall assessment is positive but not unreserved: I believe the paper is close to conference quality, but it needs tighter claims, more careful statistical exposition, and stronger robustness analysis around the API audit.

The most important revisions I would request are the following. First, narrow the causal claims: the method detects distributional non-equality under a specified interface and prompt distribution; it does not by itself identify why. Second, fix the mathematical imprecision around MMD versus squared MMD and the triangle inequality discussion. Third, justify or revise the repeated-testing and thresholding protocol used for endpoint failure decisions. Fourth, add robustness checks for prompt-template/interface mismatch in the API audit, since this is central to the paper’s headline findings. Fifth, better characterize the limitations of the Hamming kernel, ideally with a synthetic counterexample and discussion of when richer kernels may be needed.

If these issues are addressed, I expect the paper would make a valuable contribution. It tackles a real problem that is only becoming more important, and it provides a concrete, usable methodology rather than just a conceptual warning. Even where I am skeptical, the skepticism is mostly about interpretation and calibration, not about whether the underlying problem is worth studying or whether the proposed approach has promise.

My recommendation would be a weak accept to borderline accept in its current form, with the caveat that the final version should substantially tighten the claims and address the statistical and robustness concerns above.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper formulates auditing black-box LLM APIs as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem, termed Model Equality Testing, where one tests whether an API-served distribution matches a reference model distribution. The authors propose MMD-based tests with several string kernels and argue that a simple Hamming kernel over completions is especially sample-efficient. Through simulations on quantization, watermarking, finetuning, and model-swap scenarios, they report strong empirical power with relatively few samples. They then audit 31 commercial endpoints serving Llama-family models and find that 11 endpoints appear distributionally different from Meta’s released reference weights (or fp16 variants). The paper also uses estimated MMD values as effect-size measures and to compare similarity across model families.
strengths: Timely and practically important problem: black-box API auditing for LLMs is highly relevant for reproducibility, benchmarking, and user trust.
Clear problem formalization as a two-sample test over prompt-completion distributions, which unifies several auditing settings such as provider substitution and temporal drift.
Use of MMD is well motivated for high-dimensional structured outputs, and the prompt-conditioned kernel factorization is intuitive.
Strong empirical breadth: the paper evaluates quantization, watermarking, finetuning, model swaps, and real commercial APIs across multiple models and prompt sets.
The Hamming-kernel approach is simple, computationally efficient, and appears empirically effective in low-sample regimes.
The paper goes beyond binary testing by estimating effect sizes/distances between models and APIs, which is useful in practice.
Open-sourcing code and a large completion dataset increases reproducibility and likely impact.
weaknesses: The central method relies on a non-characteristic kernel (Hamming), so failure to reject does not imply equality and even rejection semantics are limited to marginal token-position discrepancies rather than full distributional equality.

Several claims are stronger than what the methodology supports; in practice the paper detects differences under a chosen kernel and prompt distribution, not true model equality in a distribution-free sense.

The empirical setup depends heavily on pre-collected samples, specific prompts, temperature-1 decoding, and matched chat templates; generalization to other decoding settings or prompt distributions is not established.

The real-API audit may conflate provider-side model changes with mismatches in prompting templates, tokenizer/character rendering, stop conditions, hidden system prompts, safety layers, or undocumented decoding defaults.

The decision rule for API failure uses repeated tests and a threshold on average rejection rate, but the statistical meaning of this aggregation is not rigorously justified as a formal level-controlled test.

The paper emphasizes sample efficiency, but some comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples because null calibration for the main MMD test uses extensive additional sampling from the reference distribution.

The practical significance of detected deviations is only partially characterized; correlation with HumanEval accuracy is moderate and many detected differences may not correspond to meaningful downstream degradation.
methodological_flaws: There is a mathematical error in Appendix A.1: the paper states that MMD 'satisfies triangle inequality, since MMD(P1,P3)=MMD(P1,P2)+MMD(P2,P3)'. This equality is false in general. Standard triangle inequality applies to the square-root MMD (the RKHS norm), not to squared MMD as defined in Equation (3). Since the paper defines MMD as a squared distance, the claim that it is a metric/pseudometric is incorrect as stated.

Relatedly, the paper repeatedly refers to the Hamming MMD as a pseudometric and to universal-kernel MMD as a metric, but with the squared formulation in Eq. (3) this is not generally true. This is a substantive mathematical imprecision affecting interpretation of the reported 'distances'.

The composite-null testing argument in Section 5 only shows a loose upper bound for the conjunction rule, but the overall audit procedure actually includes repeated runs and a fail-if-average-rejection-rate>=0.5 heuristic. The paper does not provide a proof that this final aggregated procedure controls Type I error at the claimed level.

The API audit may suffer from uncontrolled confounding: providers can differ in hidden system prompts, prompt formatting, truncation, safety filters, caching, or temperature implementation. Although the paper attempts template matching, this does not isolate the cause of detected differences, so conclusions about quantization/watermarking/substitution are not causally identified.

Empirical validity is limited by temporal nonstationarity in API sampling: some endpoint samples were collected over multiple days, while APIs may drift over time. This can inflate apparent differences unrelated to the intended provider-vs-reference comparison.

The use of character-space comparisons for cross-tokenizer settings is pragmatic but changes the tested object substantially; differences in detokenization conventions, whitespace normalization, or Unicode handling can induce detectable shifts that are not model-distribution differences in token space.
Power estimates for some baselines are based on fewer simulations/null draws (e.g., all-substrings kernel), making comparisons somewhat uneven and potentially noisy.

The paper sometimes interprets estimated Hamming MMD as an effect size comparable across settings, but because the kernel is task-, length-, and representation-dependent, such comparisons should be made more cautiously.
